'Just want to check-in if this is a good time to discuss that move' is a time check, not an agenda opener
Never asked whether he needs packing services — a furniture-only storage move still warrants the ask, especially with glass furniture in the load

Identified the inventory gap out loud ('it's a little bit difficult for us to assess how long it's gonna take unless we have an inventory list') but never worked the problem on the call — did not walk the two units item by item to build one
What's-included list was incomplete — covered two men, truck, taxes and credit card fees, but not gas, wrap, pads, bands, or tools
Disassembly/reassembly waved off rather than assessed — 'no this assembly, but it's a storage storage, so we should be good with that' — storage furniture frequently needs breakdown
No-hidden-fees pitch was partial: named credit card fees and assembly fees but not fuel surcharge or transportation fees

Estimate defaulted to the top of a very wide range — quoted 5.5 to 7.5 hours ($1,274 to $1,710) and then closed with 'I'll just keep it at seven and a half hours' for a load described as one desk and chair from one unit plus some main furniture, no boxes, heaviest item a TV console, both pickups ground-floor with door-side parking, 30 feet at the destination
Drive time between Frisco and Cedar Springs in Dallas never explained as billable clock time on a two-location move — the $75 travel fee was covered, the on-the-clock drive was not
Traffic never mentioned despite a Friday Frisco-to-Dallas leg

Save Your Ass prep speech absent — no consolidation examples, no 'take a carload' tip, no 'does that make sense?' close on that section; the carload tip was sitting right there when he said he would go through the remaining unit contents himself after the furniture was hauled out
Never mentioned the bolded detail list at the top of the confirmation email
Never asked 'any other questions before I let you go?' — she had already said 'thank you bye' when the customer had to interject with his deposit and payment question
No business hours or phone number given — only 'give us a call'
No 60-cent-per-pound baseline alongside the No Worries coverage
The 500-pound weight limit was asserted with no explanation of what happens if an item exceeds it

top_strength: The pricing and clock block was close to textbook and should be used as a model for the team. Joanna hit the 'it's super simple' opener, then gave the rate correctly and completely — '$109 per hour, per mover. So for two men it's $218 per hour' — naming the Friday tier and the per-mover math in one breath, which is exactly where most reps get vague. She then landed all three differentiators back to back: No Worries at 'up to $2,000... for any repair replacement reimbursement for any accidental damages', Meet Your Mover with a genuinely good ad-lib ('we don't take daily contract workers and we send you their names ahead of time'), and the On-Time Guarantee. She also went four-for-four on the clock — starts on arrival at the pickup location when the contract opens, two-and-a-half hour minimum, fifteen-minute intervals after that with 'we don't charge you for the full hour right away', and closed it with 'Does that make sense?' Her discovery also included the stressor question verbatim and used the school bus equivalent for the 30-foot walk.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: never default to the top of the range. Joanna, you correctly diagnosed the problem on the call — 'it's a little bit difficult for us to assess how long it's gonna take unless we have an inventory list' — and then instead of solving it you booked him at 7.5 hours and $1,710 for a desk, a chair, and some main furniture with no boxes. The fix is to build the inventory right there: 'Let's do this quickly — walk me through unit one, then unit two. What's in each?' Two minutes of that gets you a defensible number. If he genuinely cannot list it, book the realistic middle and say so: 'Based on what you've described I'd expect four to five hours, and I've built the estimate at five — you only pay for what we use.' Booking at the ceiling to protect yourself is the exact behavior driving our estimate-accuracy gap, and it inflates the quote a price-shopping customer sees. Second priority: you skipped Save Your Ass entirely and he handed you the opening — he said he would go through the leftover unit contents himself after the furniture was hauled out. That is the carload moment: 'One tip that saves people real money — anything small enough to fit in your car, take it yourself. Every load the guys don't carry is time off your bill. Make sense?' Third, smaller: he had to chase you with the deposit question after you'd already said goodbye. Add 'Any other questions before I let you go?' plus your hours and number to your close, and that catch happens on your terms.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and natural — used 'Nicholas' four times, offered 'no worries', 'that's fine', 'I'd be glad to review it for you', asked about stressors unprompted, and the customer stayed comfortable and responsive throughout ('No, that sounds good', 'Perfect'); held back from a 5 by a long uninterrupted pricing monologue, no real rapport or humor moment, and starting the farewell before he was finished asking questions.
